featured.name: terminal-digital-twin
featured.title: Container terminal digital twin
featured.summary: Simulates an automated container terminal and compares ways of dispatching its robot trucks, with a live 3D view.
featured.caveat: A simulation: no AGV congestion or yard-crane travel, so absolute throughput is an upper bound.

visual.alt: 3D view of a container terminal: four quay cranes at the berth with two vessels, eight yard blocks stacked with coloured containers, and AGVs driving between them, with control and KPI panels on either side.
visual.caption: The visualiser seven simulated hours in, Hungarian dispatch policy. docs/screenshot.png

metrics.label: moves per berth-hour, Hungarian dispatch vs nearest-idle, 4 AGVs (95 % CI +8.09 to +9.47, 10 paired seeds)
time quay cranes wait for an AGV, same comparison
simulation speed, one thread, 4 AGVs (2.22 ms per 7,604-event run)

detail.problem: In an automated terminal, quay cranes stall whenever no AGV is there to take the next container. Which AGV should serve which crane job, and when, decides how fast a vessel is turned around. Comparing dispatch rules fairly needs a simulator that gives identical results for the same seed, and policies that only see what a real terminal would know.
approach: A discrete-event core orders events by (time, sequence number) and gives each subsystem its own random stream, so the same seed gives byte-identical output headless, sliced into steps, or driven by the window.
Three dispatch policies: nearest idle AGV, due-time greedy, and a hand-written Hungarian assignment re-solved at every dispatch decision over a rolling horizon.
Runs are paired by seed and reported with confidence intervals and p-values; the report lists where a policy is worse, not only where it wins.
What-if experiments add crane breakdowns, an arrival surge and a fleet-size sweep; outages run on calendar time so they are identical across policies.

decision.title: Policies see expectations only
decision.body: Dispatch policies get mean cycle times and forecasts, never the sampled durations the simulator will actually use. That stops any policy from winning with information a real terminal would not have, at the cost of making every policy look a little worse than an oracle.

the same comparison with 6 AGVs
the same comparison with 12 AGVs: Hungarian costs a little when AGVs are plentiful

featured.name: mapf-fleet-planner
featured.title: Multi-robot fleet planner
featured.summary: Plans collision-free routes for up to 100 robots sharing a grid, and checks every plan with a separate validator.

visual.alt: Animated grid map with walls. Twenty coloured discs move through narrow doorways between rooms, each stopping inside the square of its own colour.
visual.caption: 20 robots on the room-32-32-4 map, planned by CBS and validated before export. docs/replay.svg

metrics.label: solved plans rejected by the independent validator, across 2,000 benchmark runs
solved at 50 % or better on all 5 MovingAI maps by ECBS w=1.5; optimal CBS stops at 10–40
low-level search speed-up from a bucket queue and arena vs the std::set baseline (prioritized planning)

detail.problem: Warehouse and port fleets need many robots to reach their goals without colliding or swapping through each other. The joint search space grows exponentially with the number of robots, and a plan that is fast but subtly wrong is worse than no plan.
approach: Three planners behind one library: prioritized planning, optimal Conflict-Based Search (CBS) and bounded-suboptimal ECBS, all sharing one templated low-level focal search.
Every plan is checked by a validator that shares no code or types with the planners; CBS is also checked against a brute-force joint-state Dijkstra on small maps.
A benchmark over the standard MovingAI maps, 10 to 100 agents, 10 scenarios each, with Python bindings and an animated SVG replay.
Search optimisations (binary heap, bucket queue, arena, struct-of-arrays) are runtime switches, so before/after numbers come from one binary doing identical work.

decision.title: One engine for CBS and ECBS
decision.body: With weight 1, ECBS is exactly CBS with a fewest-conflicts tie-break, so a single engine serves both and the brute-force optimality test exercises the ECBS code too. The cost is a slightly more general engine than plain CBS needs.

results.label: of 1,416 solved plans in 2,000 runs, re-checked by the validator

the same for optimal CBS

featured.name: ros2-autonomy-stack
featured.title: ROS 2 autonomy stack
featured.summary: Lets a simulated warehouse robot localise, map, plan, drive to goals and recover when its path is blocked.
featured.caveat: Runs on a custom 2D simulator, not Gazebo or a real robot: no wheel slip or sensor latency.

visual.alt: Animated top-down view of a warehouse map: the robot follows a planned path from the dock to its goal.
visual.caption: A run from the dock to the goal in the 12 × 9 m warehouse. docs/demo.gif

metrics.label: faster to the goal with Theta* + DWA than the A* + pure pursuit baseline
localisation error (ATE RMSE) at 3× sensor noise with 12 unmapped boxes
blocked-path runs where the behaviour tree's recovery still reached the goal

detail.problem: A mobile robot only navigates well if every layer works at once: odometry drifts, maps are noisy, the planned path can be blocked, and the controller has to follow the plan smoothly. Each layer has to be testable on its own and measurable together.
approach: An EKF fuses wheel odometry, IMU yaw and ICP scan matching against the prior map, with chi-square gates that reject bad matches.
Occupancy-grid mapping, A* and Theta* global planners, and pure pursuit and DWA local controllers.
A BehaviorTree.CPP v4 tree runs go-to-goal, patrol and docking, and recovers when the path is blocked.
The maths lives in ROS-free core libraries tested under sanitizers; everything builds and runs headless in Docker, and a 60-run evaluation sweeps planner, controller, noise and clutter.

decision.title: A small 2D simulator instead of Gazebo
decision.body: Gazebo needs several GB more disk and RAM and makes launch tests slow and flaky, and the metrics being evaluated are planar. The trade-off is no wheel-slip dynamics, no 3D effects and no sensor-latency model.

results.label: evaluation over seeds 1–3, 6.2 minutes of wall time
mean time to goal, Theta* + DWA vs A* + pure pursuit (17 % faster)
lower integral of curvature² along the driven path, same comparison
ATE RMSE from low noise and no clutter to 3× noise and 12 unmapped boxes; all 48 runs reached the goal
runs with a blocked-path recovery that reached the goal (91 %)

featured.name: lidar-perception-pipeline
featured.title: LiDAR perception pipeline
featured.summary: Finds and tracks cars and pedestrians in 3D LiDAR scans, frame by frame, and measures every stage.
featured.caveat: Synthetic data: every number comes from a seeded generator that writes frames in the KITTI layout. Not comparable to KITTI or any real-data benchmark.

visual.alt: Top-down LiDAR point cloud with detected objects drawn as boxes and track identifiers.
visual.caption: The viewer on synthetic sequence 0000. docs/viewer.png

metrics.label: single thread with spatial-hash clustering (brute force: 6.0 FPS), about 110k points per frame
throughput with 8 threads of frame pipelining (441.4 FPS); per-frame latency does not drop
precision / recall at IoU 0.3 with L-shape boxes (PCA baseline: 0.500 / 0.486)

detail.problem: A perception stack has to turn about 110,000 points per frame into a short list of tracked objects within a frame budget. Each stage costs time and each shortcut costs accuracy, so both have to be measured, not assumed.
approach: Stages in order: ground removal, 0.2 m voxel downsampling, Euclidean or DBSCAN clustering, 3D box fitting, then Kalman-filter tracking with Hungarian assignment.
Three neighbour-search structures for clustering (brute force, k-d tree, spatial hash) behind one interface, timed per stage at p50 and p99.
PCA and L-shape box fitting compared on detection precision/recall, MOTA and IDF1.
Frame-level pipelining across threads; one script regenerates every result.

decision.title: Synthetic data in the KITTI layout
decision.body: KITTI, nuScenes, Waymo and PandaSet all need an account to download. A seeded ray-cast generator writes frames in the KITTI tracking layout, and the real KITTI loader reads them unchanged. Results are reproducible, but they come from idealised geometry, so the L-shape gain in particular is a best case.

results.label: total p50 / p99 latency per frame, spatial hash, 1 thread
clustering p50, brute force vs spatial hash
precision / recall at IoU 0.5, L-shape (PCA: 0.269 / 0.261)
MOTA / IDF1 with L-shape boxes (simplified definitions in the README)
8 threads, frame pipelining; MOTA and IDF1 identical for every thread count

featured.name: core-banking-ledger
featured.title: Core banking ledger
featured.summary: A banking backend that keeps every account balanced through concurrent payments, client retries and crashes mid-transfer.
featured.caveat: Measured on a laptop with one app instance; earlier runs under other load reached about 300 req/s.

visual.alt: Grafana dashboard with panels for payment throughput, saga latency percentiles and transactional-outbox lag during a load test.
visual.caption: The Grafana dashboard during the k6 load test. docs/grafana-dashboard.png

metrics.label: POST /payments under k6, 20 virtual users for 60 s, 0.00 % errors
p99 payment latency in the same run (p50 50.2 ms)
unbalanced entries or balance mismatches in the ledger audit after the run

detail.problem: Moving money is easy until two requests touch the same account at once, a client retries, or the process dies halfway through a transfer. The ledger must never create or lose money and never let an account go negative, under all three.
approach: A double-entry ledger in Postgres with signed postings and a funding account per currency, so the sum over all accounts is always zero and any created money shows up in the audit.
Payments run as an orchestrated saga: reserve a hold, post, notify, with compensation in reverse.
A transactional outbox feeds Kafka; consumers are idempotent on a unique event id, so delivery is at least once and the effect is exactly once.
JWT security, rate limiting, OpenAPI docs, Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry tracing, a Helm chart and a CI pipeline.

decision.title: Spring JDBC instead of JPA
decision.body: The ledger needs exact SQL: FOR UPDATE ordering, version-guarded updates, ON CONFLICT and SKIP LOCKED. JPA's hidden flushes and dirty checking make that harder to reason about. The cost is more hand-written SQL and mapping code.

results.label: payment requests in the 60 s k6 run, 5 % of them idempotent replays
latency p50 / p95 / p99
saga p99 from Prometheus during the run
concurrency stress test over 10 accounts: conservation held, no negative balance, clean audit
optimistic-lock retries for 3,492 committed transfers, vs 0 with pessimistic locking

media.caption: The OpenAPI documentation. docs/swagger-ui.png

featured.name: research-rag-platform
featured.title: Research paper Q&A
featured.summary: Answers questions about economics and finance papers with page-level citations, and says when the papers don't hold the answer.
featured.caveat: Answers come from a mock extractive generator, not an LLM. Retrieval numbers are real runs on a 58-question gold set.

visual.alt: Web interface showing a question about a finance paper, an answer with numbered citations, and the cited passages with their page numbers.
visual.caption: The React UI answering a question with page citations. docs/screenshot-ask.png

metrics.label: recall@10 with hybrid search and reranking (dense only: 0.647)
held-out MRR@10 of the best of 28 configurations, 5-fold cross-validated
abstention precision and recall, leave-one-out, on only 7 unanswerable questions

detail.problem: Finance papers are full of numbers, names and tables that dense embeddings blur together, and a research tool that cites the wrong page is worse than none. Retrieval quality is the bottleneck, so it has to be measured against a gold set rather than eyeballed.
approach: Ingests openly licensed World Bank working papers and arXiv q-fin preprints into PostgreSQL + pgvector.
Hybrid search: BM25, dense vectors and reciprocal-rank fusion, then a cross-encoder reranker.
Citations are checked against the passage and page before an answer reaches the user; questions the corpus can't answer are refused before generation.
One service, three front doors: a FastAPI backend, a React + TypeScript UI and an MCP server.

decision.title: Abstain on the reranker score, before generation
decision.body: If the best reranked passage scores below a threshold, the system refuses without calling a model. That saves a call and avoids asking an LLM to judge its own ignorance. The threshold rests on only 7 unanswerable questions and moved a lot under leave-one-out, and the README says so.

results.label: recall@10, BM25 alone vs hybrid + rerank (recursive chunker)
dense-only MRR@10, MiniLM vs bge-small-en-v1.5

featured.name: agentic-threat-hunter
featured.title: Agentic threat hunter
featured.summary: An agent that hunts for attacker activity in security logs through read-only tools and writes Sigma detection rules for what it finds.
featured.caveat: Every number comes from a scripted mock LLM. It shows the pipeline, tools and safeguards work end to end, not how well an LLM hunts.

visual.caption: The allow-list is applied at registration, so a disallowed tool does not exist for the client, and every call is audited.

metrics.label: attack techniques detected by the agent, vs 1/45 for a single-prompt baseline
agent findings that passed the grounding check against the logs
precision of the Sigma rules the agent proposed (micro-averaged)

detail.problem: An LLM agent with tool access to security logs is useful only if its findings are grounded in real evidence, and safe only if a hijacked model cannot do harm. Both need measuring against labelled attacks, against a fair baseline.
approach: Seeded synthetic auth, process, network and web logs with labelled MITRE ATT&CK attack chains and false-positive bait.
An MCP server with five read-only tools, an allow-list, input validation and an append-only JSONL audit log.
A planner-to-tool loop with step, token and time budgets, and a human-approval gate that only records containment actions.
A separate Sigma validator scores the rules the agent writes; the agent is compared with a single-prompt baseline and a token-matched baseline.

decision.title: Read-only tools, with the approval gate on the agent side
decision.body: The server can only read; even the rule tool only drafts and dry-runs. Containment requests go to an agent-local gate that records a human's decision and executes nothing. A hijacked model's worst tool call is a read of synthetic logs.

results.label: techniques detected: agent, baseline, token-matched baseline
findings grounded
rule precision / recall (micro)
estimated input tokens per hunt for the agent, vs 17,575 for the plain baseline
T1560.001 (archive before exfiltration) is never detected by any system

featured.name: agent-redteam-eval
featured.title: Red-team evals for AI agents
featured.summary: Attacks tool-using AI agents with prompt injection and measures what each defence actually stops.
featured.caveat: The agent's LLM and the LLM judge are mocks. Numbers show what each defence blocks, not how robust a real model is.

visual.alt: HTML report with a table of attack success rates per defence condition and target, with confidence intervals.
visual.caption: The generated HTML report. docs/report_screenshot.png

metrics.label: attack success rate on the toy agent, no defences vs all defences
goal-hijack success that remains with all defences on: the clearest gap
benign runs blocked with all defences on (12 of 36): the cost of those defences

detail.problem: Prompt injection against tool-using agents is easy to demonstrate and hard to measure. A useful harness has to score what an attack actually did (a file read, data sent out, a tool called), compare defences on the same draws, and count the benign work each defence breaks.
approach: 64 versioned seed cases (49 attacks across six categories, 15 benign tasks) plus 98 generated mutants, run under seven defence conditions and three seeds.
Two targets: a deliberately naive toy agent as a positive control, and the real agent loop and MCP server from agentic-threat-hunter.
A rule judge scores executed effects; a mock LLM judge is checked against it and against hand labels with Cohen's kappa.
Hash-keyed coin flips give every condition the same random draw, so the ablation is paired.

decision.title: Score executed effects, not intent
decision.body: An attack counts only if it changed something: a denied call needs no clean-up, so counting it would overstate risk. Near misses are still logged as denied for analysis.

results.label: toy agent ASR, no defences vs all (95 % CI 0.047–0.095)
the same for the agentic-threat-hunter agent
toy exfiltration with the output DLP filter alone
Cohen's kappa, rule judge vs mock LLM judge, toy / project-5 attack runs
benign false-positive rate with all defences, on a small n (12/36 and 9/27)

other.name: Limit_order_book
other.summary: A stock exchange order book and matching engine, checked by rebuilding every NASDAQ book from a full day of real market data.
other.note: Example: replayed a full day of NASDAQ ITCH 5.0 (268,744,780 messages) at 6.72 M msg/s on one pinned core, with 0 of 263,241,937 top-of-book mismatches against an independent reference book.

other.name: Market_Data_Feed_Handler_UDP
other.summary: Receives a replayed NASDAQ feed over UDP multicast, recovers lost packets, and keeps its order books identical to the exchange's.
other.note: Example: median wire-to-book latency of 1,904 ns, and 7 of 7 loss scenarios ended with books identical to the publisher's.

other.name: cpp-latency-lab
other.summary: Nine small C++ experiments on caches, branch prediction, memory layout, dispatch and false sharing. Each prediction was written down before measuring, and the wrong ones are listed.
other.note: Example: with fetch_add, two threads sharing a cache line made each increment about 4× slower.

other.name: seam-carving
other.summary: Content-aware image resizing with dynamic-programming, greedy and graph-cut seam finders. A six-person team assignment: I built the base (CMake, energy map, dynamic-programming seam finder, carving loop and command-line tool).
